Class ScrollContainer

java.lang.Object
com.trevlar.menukit.api.element.AbstractPanelElement
com.trevlar.menukit.api.element.ScrollContainer
All Implemented Interfaces:
PanelElement
public class ScrollContainer extends AbstractPanelElement
A clipped viewport over pre-positioned elements, scrolled vertically: the single primitive for "show content larger than its bounds". 
ScrollContainer.builder().size(140, 80)
        .content(rows)                      // positioned from the viewport's top-left
        .build();

Single responsibility

It owns clipping, the scroll position, the scrollbar and routing input to its children. It does not lay out: children are placed from the viewport's top-left (compose them with Row/Column or give positions), and the viewport's size is declared. Width reserved for the scrollbar lane is viewportWidthFor(int).

A child that grows pushes the children below it down, as on a panel (7.3.0): a ListView a row is added to, an open Section, a wrapped label, by its PanelElement.extraLayoutHeight(), and back up as it shrinks, read every frame, so the scroll range follows in the same frame. A settings page that scrolls (a list, then more settings) places what follows the list as if it took no room.

The scrollbar shows only while there is something to scroll (7.3.0)

In both looks the track and handle are drawn only while the content is taller than the viewport; while everything fits the lane is empty and takes no clicks. A container that lays its own children out (ScrollContainer.Builder.fitWidth()) also gives them the lane's width back while it is hidden, so rows reach the right edge and the margins either side match; it lays them out again the frame the content starts or stops overflowing. A wider layout is never taller, and a narrower one never shorter, so the choice settles at once and never flips back and forth. Children placed by hand keep the width they were given.

Scroll position: view state, or the consumer's

By default the scroll is the container's own view state, as a Tabs body's is. state(get, set) hands it to the consumer instead, in pixels from the top: get is read every frame, set receives each change. Pixels, not a fraction: when the content changes height while shown (a section opening), what is on screen stays where it is and only the range changes. That holds for a child above the window too: one that grows or shrinks there moves the scroll by as much, so the first child reaching into the window stays put. A position past the new end is clamped, and the clamp written back. Nothing else moves it: no click on a child scrolls it into view, and it never glides (the wheel and the handle move it at once), so a content change has no glide target to fight. The one exception (7.3.0): a child that asks to be shown (PanelElement.takeRevealRequest(), a ListView whose selection moved) is scrolled into view, the least distance, at once.

Input

The wheel over the viewport scrolls it, SCROLL_PIXELS_PER_TICK pixels a notch (after any child that scrolls itself, a nested container, had the wheel); dragging the handle scrolls it, and a press on the track jumps the handle there and holds it, as vanilla's lists do; clicks inside the viewport reach the children at their scrolled positions; the scrollbar lane eats its own clicks. An open popover of a child (a Dropdown) claims its whole area, even the part hanging below the viewport, and draws unclipped on the overlay pass. Disabled (its own disabledWhen or its panel's), it and everything in it are grayed and inert.

Every child is dispatched through ChildDispatch, with the context moved to the scrolled content origin: the same order a panel uses.

Slots (7.2.0)

A slot element among the children (SlotKit's) scrolls and clips like any child. One wholly out of view is not rendered, so its slot is parked. One across the viewport's top or bottom edge keeps its real position, so nothing beside it moves, and is cut at the edge: vanilla draws only the part inside, and only that part hovers and takes clicks (the element reports its slot with api.host.SlotClip). Under an opaque panel, the part inside is the panel's own slot; the part past the edge is the panel's, like a gap between slots.

In the Default look

In the Default look (ScreenKind.DEFAULT) it is the band every Options screen has: vanilla's darker list background behind the content, scrolling with it, vanilla's separator along the top and the bottom, drawn in the 2 px just outside the container as vanilla draws them, and vanilla's thin list scroller (widget/scroller on widget/scroller_background) at the right of the lane, hidden while everything fits. The lane, the handle's size and travel and the input are the same in both looks.

One scroller

The scroll model (pixels, clamping, the wheel's step, the drag) and the scrollbar's drawing are MenuKit's one scroller, core.Scroller, which a Tabs strip scrolls by too: its sidebar's scrollbar is this one, the same handle and track at the same size.

The band also insets its content as vanilla's lists do: the children's origin is DEFAULT_INSET_X in from the left and DEFAULT_INSET_Y down, with as much room past the last child, scrolling with the content. The right needs no inset of its own: the scrollbar lane already keeps the content clear of the scroller. So the content is narrower in the Default look: size it with viewportWidthFor(int, ScreenKind). A Tabs page and a panel's own auto-scroll do that for their children.

In a dialog (a modal panel, PanelElement.inDialog(boolean)) the frame and its padding are already the margin, so the band insets its content by the dialog's own gap, DIALOG_INSET, on every side it insets, not the full screen's. One rule for every band (bandInsetX(ScreenKind, boolean), bandInsetY(ScreenKind, boolean)): this one, a Tabs page, a panel's auto-scroll.

Sized to its content (7.2.0)

ScrollContainer.Builder.fitWidth() makes it as wide as its widest child plus the band's inset and the scrollbar lane, so a grid of whole columns is never cut off on either look; given more room by its panel it takes it, and lays its children out to it (a child that centers itself stays centered). ScrollContainer.Builder.fitHeight() makes the declared height the most it is: as tall as its content up to that, scrolling past it. Its height then follows its content, so it pushes what is below it as a ListView does (7.3.0): its whole height is its PanelElement.extraLayoutHeight(), so place what follows as if it took no room, and that moves down as the content grows and back up as it shrinks, in the same frame.

A lane outside its width (7.4.0)

ScrollContainer.Builder.laneOutside() puts the scrollbar lane beside the declared width instead of inside it: the content keeps the whole declared width, and the container is a lane wider only while the lane shows. So whatever holds it makes room for the scrollbar exactly while there is one, as the container list widens its frame for a section's own scrolling grid.

Fitting the room (7.4.0)

ScrollContainer.Builder.fitRoom(int) makes it as tall as its content while there is room, and shorter only when there is not, in whole steps (rows), never below its declared height. In a ContainerRegion section the region asks it to give back what the list would overflow the screen by (PanelElement.yieldHeight(int)), so it shows every row and no scrollbar while the window has the height, and scrolls once it is too short; with ScrollContainer.Builder.laneOutside() the lane takes width only while it scrolls. Elsewhere nothing asks, and it is as tall as its content. It pushes what is below it as ScrollContainer.Builder.fitHeight() does.

Filling its container (7.3.0)

ScrollContainer.Builder.fillHeight() takes the height its container gives it instead: what a panel's viewport leaves below it, what a vertical Flow has left after its other children, the whole of a Tabs page. A header above it stays put while only it scrolls. On a Tabs page it draws no band of its own (inBand): the page's band is behind it already.

    • DEFAULT_INSET_X

      public static final int DEFAULT_INSET_X
      In the Default look, how far in from the list band's left edge its content starts (and, in a Tabs page that does not scroll, how far from its right edge it ends): vanilla's gap between a list row's content and the list's scrollbar. 26.2's AbstractSelectionList.scrollBarX() is getRowRight() + scrollbarWidth() + 2 (6 + 2), and a row's content ends Entry.CONTENT_PADDING (2) inside the row, so 10; Controls' KeyBindsList.KeyEntry ends its last button at scrollBarX() - 10. MenuKit adds 4 to that: a settings page of labels, headings and wrapped text read cramped at vanilla's 10, whose lists hold only buttons.
      See Also:
      • Constant Field Values

    • DEFAULT_INSET_Y

      public static final int DEFAULT_INSET_Y
      In the Default look, the room above the band's first child and below its last: vanilla's list padding (AbstractSelectionList.getFirstEntryY() is the list's top + 2, contentHeight() the rows + 4) plus a row's Entry.CONTENT_PADDING (2), which is 4. MenuKit uses 10: at 4 the first heading sat on the band's top separator. It scrolls with the content, as vanilla's does.
      See Also:

      Whether this element handles pointer input, so a point on it is a solid claim on a transparent panel. Controls return true; render-only decorations keep the false default, so they never eat a click they do nothing with.

      Renders this element at (ctx.originX() + getChildX(), ctx.originY() + getChildY()). When ctx.disabled() is true, an element draws its disabled look.

    • getActiveOverlayBounds

      public int @Nullable [] getActiveOverlayBounds(InputContext in)
      Description copied from interface: PanelElement
      The screen-space bounds [x, y, width, height] of this element's active overlay (an open popover), or null when none is open. The dispatcher gives an element whose overlay contains the event exclusive ownership of that click or scroll, before any hit test, and the claim rule treats the overlay as claimed whatever the panel's opacity.
      Parameters:
      in - the element's input context (its origin, so it can place the overlay)

    • notifyClickOutsideOverlay

      public void notifyClickOutsideOverlay(InputContext in)
      Description copied from interface: PanelElement
      Tells an element with transient open state (a popover) that a click landed somewhere it did not claim, so it can close. The dispatchers call it on every shown element for every click, even one another element consumed; each element decides for itself whether the click was outside. Default: no-op.

      A mouse click on this element (the dispatcher hit-tested first). Returns true if consumed, stopping dispatch to other elements, slots and vanilla. button is vanilla's; compare it with Click.LEFT, Click.RIGHT and Click.MIDDLE. Default: false.
